questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Match the following causes of hypothyroidism to the source's grouping — 1) Iatrogenic 2) Drug-induced 3) Iodine-related 4) Autoimmune/other … A) Post-thyroidectomy / post-radioiodine B) Lithium, amiodarone, interferon-α, immune checkpoint inhibitors C) Iodine deficiency / excess D) Hashimoto thyroiditis, infiltrative disease
questions.exp: The page clusters iatrogenic (post-surgery, post-RAI), drugs (lithium, amiodarone, IFN-α, ICIs), iodine (deficiency or excess), and autoimmune/other causes (Hashimoto, infiltrative). (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: A bipolar patient on lithium develops overt hypothyroidism one year after starting therapy. Which mechanism best fits the source?
opts: Lithium increases TSH receptor antibody binding
questions.exp: Lithium inhibits thyroid-hormone release and can also cause goitre; the page lists it under drug-induced hypothyroidism. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Assess these drug-induced statements: I Interferon-α can cause irreversible hypothyroidism. II Amiodarone causes hypothyroidism only via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.
questions.exp: IFN-α's thyroid effects are usually reversible after stopping; amiodarone causes hypothyroidism by multiple mechanisms, not only Wolff-Chaikoff. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a drug not on the source's hypothyroid list?
questions.exp: Lithium, amiodarone and IFN-α are listed as causes of hypothyroidism; propranolol only treats thyrotoxic symptoms. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: The single most common worldwide cause of hypothyroidism on this page is ___.
questions.exp: Iodine deficiency is the global leader; in iodine-replete countries Hashimoto dominates. The page explicitly calls out iodine deficiency first. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Match the following endocrine disorder to its expected thyroid phenotype on the page — 1) Bipolar disorder on lithium 2) Patient receiving IFN-α for hepatitis C 3) Patient receiving amiodarone 4) Newborn in iodine-deficient region … A) Acquired hypothyroidism B) Often reversible thyroiditis C) Can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism (Type 1 vs 2) D) Endemic cretinism
questions.exp: Lithium causes acquired hypothyroidism; IFN-α usually produces reversible thyroiditis; amiodarone can produce either Type 1 or Type 2 patterns; severe iodine deficiency causes endemic cretinism. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: A patient on amiodarone develops overt hypothyroidism; uptake scan shows high iodine uptake with elevated IL-6. Which amiodarone type is most consistent?
questions.exp: Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis is destructive thyroiditis with low uptake and high IL-6; hypothyroidism with high uptake and raised IL-6 sits in the destructive pattern. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Assess amiodarone: I It can produce both hypothyroidism and thyrotoxicosis. II Type 1 is a destructive thyroiditis.
questions.exp: Amiodarone causes both hypothyroidism and thyrotoxicosis; Type 1 is iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, Type 2 is destructive thyroiditis. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Match the following clinical feature of hypothyroidism to its system — 1) Cold intolerance, weight gain 2) Bradycardia, pericardial effusion 3) Menorrhagia, galactorrhoea 4) Carpal tunnel syndrome … A) Constitutional B) Cardiovascular C) Reproductive D) Musculoskeletal / neurological
questions.exp: Cold intolerance and weight gain are constitutional; bradycardia and pericardial effusion are cardiovascular; menorrhagia and galactorrhoea are reproductive; carpal tunnel syndrome is musculoskeletal/neurological. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with weight gain, cold intolerance and menorrhagia. The least likely coexisting finding on this page is:
questions.exp: Exophthalmos is a feature of Graves thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism; carpal tunnel, bradycardia and hypercholesterolaemia all appear in the hypothyroid features list. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: On the source's clinical-feature diagram, the least common but most pathognomonic neuropsychiatric feature of severe hypothyroidism is ___.
questions.exp: Hashimoto encephalopathy is the rare but pathognomonic CNS complication; the other items are common but not pathognomonic. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Evaluate hypothyroidism clinical features: I Pleural and pericardial effusions occur. II Obstructive sleep apnoea is associated.
questions.exp: The page lists pleural and pericardial effusions plus obstructive sleep apnoea among hypothyroid features. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among causes of primary hypothyroidism listed on the page?
questions.exp: Secondary (central) hypothyroidism is not a primary thyroid failure and is grouped separately; the other three are primary gland failure. (Book p905)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Match the following Hashimoto features to the source's annotation — 1) Pathology 2) Most affected demographic 3) Typical antibody 4) Standard Rx in adult … A) Lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centres and Hürthle cells B) Middle-aged women C) Anti-TPO (and anti-thyroglobulin) D) Levothyroxine replacement
questions.exp: The page describes lymphocytic infiltrates with Hürthle cells, predominance in middle-aged women, anti-TPO as the marker, and levothyroxine replacement. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: A 38-year-old woman has a firm rubbery goitre with anti-TPO antibody titres of 800 IU/mL and subclinical hypothyroidism. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.exp: High anti-TPO with goitre in a middle-aged woman fits Hashimoto; Graves would have TSH-receptor antibodies and ophthalmopathy. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Evaluate these Hashimoto facts: I Anti-TPO is the most sensitive antibody. II Hashimoto is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete regions.
questions.exp: Anti-TPO is highlighted as the sensitive marker, and the page notes Hashimoto as the leading cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Histologically, the lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centres in Hashimoto is accompanied by ___ cells.
questions.exp: Hürthle (Askanazy) cells are the oxyphilic change characteristic of Hashimoto. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Match the following antibody to the source's typical association — 1) Anti-TPO 2) Anti-thyroglobulin 3) TSH-receptor antibody … A) Hashimoto thyroiditis B) Hashimoto thyroiditis (less specific) C) Graves disease
questions.exp: Anti-TPO is the sensitive marker for Hashimoto; anti-thyroglobulin is also seen but is less specific; TSH-receptor antibodies point to Graves. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: A Hashimoto patient with TSH 5.4 mIU/L and normal free T4 is asymptomatic. The most consistent management is:
questions.exp: Mild subclinical hypothyroidism without symptoms and free T4 normal is monitored; treatment thresholds depend on TSH level and antibodies. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Assess subclinical hypothyroidism: I It is defined by raised TSH with normal free T4. II Treatment threshold is the same for every adult patient.
questions.exp: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined by raised TSH with normal free T4, but treatment thresholds vary with age, antibodies, pregnancy and cardiovascular risk. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among the source's TSH-guided treatment thresholds for subclinical hypothyroidism?
opts: Treat only if TSH > 10 mIU/L regardless of antibodies
questions.exp: Universal levothyroxine in pregnancy with TSH > 2.5, antibody-positive patients > 5, and cardiac patients > 7 are individualised thresholds; the 'wait until > 10' rule is an oversimplification. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: In pregnancy, the source-stated upper limit for first-trimester TSH is approximately ___ mIU/L.
questions.exp: Pregnancy-specific TSH targets are stricter; the first-trimester upper limit is approximately 2.5 mIU/L. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Match the following population with the source's treatment approach for subclinical hypothyroidism — 1) Older adult with TSH 6 mIU/L 2) Young symptomatic woman 3) Pregnant with TSH 3.1 mIU/L 4) Hashimoto with TSH 12 mIU/L … A) Often observe B) Treat C) Treat (lower target) D) Treat (high-risk)
questions.exp: Older adults are often observed; young symptomatic patients are treated; pregnancy targets are stricter; overt-range Hashimoto (TSH > 10) is treated. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester has TSH 3.4 mIU/L with positive anti-TPO antibodies. Which intervention is most consistent with the source?
questions.exp: First-trimester TSH should be kept below ~2.5 mIU/L; antibodies and pregnancy warrant levothyroxine replacement. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Which antibody is highlighted as the most sensitive serologic marker for Hashimoto thyroiditis?
questions.exp: Anti-TPO is the most sensitive marker per the page; anti-thyroglobulin is less sensitive. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
questions.q: Assess antibody findings: I Anti-thyroglobulin is occasionally positive in healthy adults. II Hashimoto never coexists with Graves disease.
questions.exp: Anti-thyroglobulin can be present in healthy individuals; rare overlap of Hashimoto and Graves pathology does occur, although uncommon. (Book p906)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Match the following complication to its source description — 1) Myxoedema coma 2) Hashimoto encephalopathy 3) Carpal tunnel syndrome 4) Hypocholesterolaemia (printed label, unusual) … A) Decompensated severe hypothyroidism B) Steroid-responsive neuropsychiatric syndrome C) Most common cause in females D) Cardiovascular risk-related feature (page label)
questions.exp: Myxoedema coma is decompensated severe hypothyroidism; Hashimoto encephalopathy is a steroid-responsive neuropsychiatric syndrome; CTS is the most common cause in females per the page; hypocholesterolaemia is the page's own label (note: hypothyroid patients typically have hypercholesterolaemia, an inconsistency the source labels as 'hypocholesterolaemia'). (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: An 80-year-old woman is found hypothermic, bradycardic and obtunded in winter; TSH is markedly elevated. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Decompensated severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia and obtundation fits myxoedema coma. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Assess myxoedema coma: I It carries a high mortality even with treatment. II IV levothyroxine plus glucocorticoids is a typical emergency regimen.
questions.exp: Myxoedema coma has high mortality; empiric IV levothyroxine (often combined with liothyronine) plus stress-dose hydrocortisone is the source's emergency regimen. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among complications where hypothyroidism affects the central nervous system?
questions.exp: Hypocholesterolaemia is a metabolic label, not a CNS complication; the others are neurological. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Per the page's most-common-cause note, carpal tunnel syndrome in females is most often caused by ___.
questions.exp: The page states hypothyroidism is the most common cause of CTS in females, with amyloidosis as the most common cause in males. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Match the following effusions/comorbidities to the source's hypothyroid complications list — 1) Pleural 2) Pericardial 3) Ascites 4) Oligomenorrhoea … A) Serous cavity collection B) Reproductive disturbance C) Refractory to diuretics per source D) Same column
questions.exp: Pleural and pericardial effusions are common serous cavity collections; ascites is sometimes refractory to diuretics per the page; oligomenorrhoea / amenorrhoea is a reproductive disturbance. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: A hypothyroid patient has recurrent large-volume pleural and pericardial effusions that do not improve with diuretics. Which mechanism is most consistent with the source?
opts: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
questions.exp: Hypothyroid effusions are typically myxoedematous, with high protein content and poor response to diuretics. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Assess cardiac effects: I Hypothyroidism causes bradycardia. II Pericardial effusion is a recognised complication.
questions.exp: Bradycardia and pericardial effusion are both listed; long-standing hypothyroidism can cause pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade rarely. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Match the following complication to the most likely clinical context — 1) Obstructive sleep apnoea 2) Carpal tunnel syndrome 3) Myxoedema coma 4) Hashimoto encephalopathy … A) Common in obese hypothyroid adults B) Most common cause of CTS in females C) Decompensated hypothyroid with hypothermia D) Steroid-responsive neuropsychiatric syndrome
questions.exp: OSA is common in obese hypothyroid adults; CTS in females is mostly due to hypothyroidism; myxoedema coma presents with hypothermia; Hashimoto encephalopathy is the steroid-responsive neuropsychiatric syndrome. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: A 70-year-old hypothyroid on levothyroxine has increasing pericardial effusion. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Assess cardiac tamponade and ensure euthyroidism
Increase methimazole to lower TSH further
questions.exp: Effusions can progress even on treatment; assess haemodynamics (tamponade) and ensure adequate replacement rather than stopping therapy. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Atypical pericardial effusion that is high-protein and slow-accumulating in hypothyroid patients is called ___.
questions.exp: Myxoedema pericardial effusion is the eponymous hypothyroid entity; it can be large but tamponade is uncommon. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
questions.q: Assess the source's gender note: I Hypothyroidism is the most common cause of CTS in females. II Amyloidosis is the most common cause of CTS in males per the source.
questions.exp: Both statements reflect the page's gender-stratified most-common-cause list for carpal tunnel syndrome. (Book p907)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Match the following principles of levothyroxine therapy — 1) Form 2) Dosing starting point 3) Administration timing 4) Monitoring interval … A) Oral levothyroxine (tablets) B) Weight-based 1.6 µg/kg in young, low in elderly/cardiac C) Empty stomach, before breakfast D) 6–8 weeks after dose change
questions.exp: Oral levothyroxine is given once daily on an empty stomach; full replacement is 1.6 µg/kg in healthy young adults, lower in elderly or cardiac patients; TSH is rechecked 6–8 weeks after dose changes. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with overt hypothyroidism is started on levothyroxine 100 µg daily. What monitoring schedule fits the source?
opts: Check TSH 6–8 weeks after each dose change
Check TSH monthly for the first year
No monitoring needed once symptoms improve
questions.exp: TSH is checked 6–8 weeks after every dose change until stable, then every 6–12 months. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Evaluate levothyroxine administration: I It should be taken with breakfast for best absorption. II Calcium and iron supplements reduce its absorption.
questions.exp: Levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast; calcium, iron, antacids and certain foods reduce its absorption. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a drug that reduces levothyroxine absorption?
questions.exp: Methimazole is an antithyroid drug, not an absorption blocker; calcium, iron and PPIs all interfere with levothyroxine uptake. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: In healthy young adults, the typical full replacement dose of levothyroxine is approximately ___ µg/kg/day.
questions.exp: Approximately 1.6 µg/kg/day in young healthy adults; lower doses in elderly or ischaemic heart disease. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Match the following patient group with the source's levothyroxine starting approach — 1) Young healthy adult 2) Elderly 3) Ischaemic heart disease 4) Pregnancy … A) Full weight-based dose B) Start low (25–50 µg), titrate slowly C) Start very low, titrate by 12.5 µg D) Increase dose 25–30% over pre-pregnancy dose
questions.exp: Young healthy adults receive full weight-based replacement; elderly start low and titrate slowly; cardiac patients start very low and increment by 12.5 µg; pregnancy increases the dose by 25–30%. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: An 80-year-old with atrial fibrillation and overt hypothyroidism needs levothyroxine. The best initial regimen is:
opts: 200 µg daily as a stat dose
questions.exp: Start low in elderly cardiac patients (25–50 µg) and titrate by 12.5–25 µg every 6–8 weeks to avoid precipitating ischaemia. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Assess thyroid replacement endpoints: I In primary hypothyroidism the target is normal TSH. II In central hypothyroidism the target is normal free T4 only.
questions.exp: Primary hypothyroidism uses TSH as the target; central hypothyroidism uses free T4 in the upper normal range because TSH is unreliable. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Match the following special population to its TSH target on levothyroxine — 1) Young adult 2) Pregnancy (T1) 3) Elderly with cardiac disease 4) Pregnancy (T3) … A) 0.5–2.5 mIU/L B) 0.5–3.0 mIU/L C) Up to 4–6 mIU/L acceptable D) 0.5–2.5 mIU/L
questions.exp: Young adults aim for 0.5–2.5; both trimesters of pregnancy aim for similar low targets (T1 stricter); elderly with cardiac disease may tolerate slightly higher TSH. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: A pregnant woman on levothyroxine 100 µg now needs an increased dose. By what percentage should the source's guidance recommend an increase?
questions.exp: Pregnancy increases thyroxine requirement by 25–30%; dose should be adjusted once pregnancy is confirmed. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: The source's preferred thyroid hormone preparation is ___, with ___ reserved for selected refractory cases.
questions.exp: Levothyroxine is the standard; liothyronine is occasionally added in refractory cases but routine combination therapy is not standard. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
questions.q: Assess therapeutic drug interactions: I Levothyroxine absorption is reduced by sucralfate. II Cholestyramine reduces levothyroxine absorption.
questions.exp: Sucralfate, cholestyramine, calcium, iron and PPIs all reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate dosing by at least four hours. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Match the following follow-up plan — 1) Stable primary hypothyroidism 2) After dose change 3) Persistent symptoms despite normal TSH 4) Suspected non-compliance … A) Repeat TSH every 6–12 months B) Recheck TSH/FT3/FT4 at ~3 months C) Reassess adherence and drug interactions D) Re-evaluate diagnosis and consider T3 add-on
questions.exp: Stable patients are monitored every 6–12 months; after dose changes recheck at 3 months; symptoms despite normal TSH prompt diagnosis review and possible T3 add-on; persistent abnormal labs are commonly due to non-compliance or interactions. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: On levothyroxine 100 µg a patient's TSH remains elevated at 9 mIU/L despite claims of adherence. Which step is most consistent with the page?
opts: Assess adherence and drug interactions before increasing the dose
questions.exp: Persistent abnormal TFTs are most often due to non-compliance or interfering drugs; investigate before titrating. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Assess follow-up intervals: I Re-check at 3 months after a dose change. II Once TSH normal, taper can be attempted cautiously.
questions.exp: After dose changes, TSH is rechecked at about 3 months; once TSH normal, slow taper may be attempted in selected patients (e.g. transient thyroiditis). (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a transient cause where levothyroxine can eventually be tapered?
questions.exp: Post-thyroidectomy hypothyroidism is permanent; the others are typically transient and may allow cautious taper once TSH normal. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Relief of hypothyroid symptoms typically occurs ___ months after TSH normalises.
questions.exp: Symptomatic relief usually takes 3–6 months after biochemical normalisation; lipid and other parameters take longer. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Match the following emergency therapy for myxoedema coma — 1) First-line hormone 2) Steroid 3) Supportive measure 4) Trigger work-up … A) IV levothyroxine (often with liothyronine) B) IV hydrocortisone C) Active warming, electrolytes, ventilation D) Infection, MI, cold exposure, sedatives
questions.exp: Myxoedema coma is treated with IV levothyroxine plus hydrocortisone (until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), supportive measures (warming, ventilation) and search for triggers (infection, MI, cold, sedatives). (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: An obtunded hypothyroid patient is started on IV levothyroxine. Why is hydrocortisone added concurrently?
opts: To cover possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency
questions.exp: Concurrent adrenal insufficiency is possible; giving thyroid hormone first can precipitate adrenal crisis. Hydrocortisone is given until adrenal status is clear. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Assess myxoedema coma: I Active external rewarming is the recommended initial step. II IV levothyroxine should be withheld until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.
questions.exp: Active rewarming can precipitate arrhythmia; passive rewarming is preferred. Levothyroxine should not be withheld — both levothyroxine and hydrocortisone are started empirically. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Match the following common trigger of myxoedema coma — 1) Infection 2) Cold exposure 3) Sedatives 4) MI … A) Most common precipitant B) Winter decompensation C) CNS depressant D) Cardiovascular collapse
questions.exp: Infection is the most common trigger; cold exposure causes winter decompensation; sedatives depress CNS; MI can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: A hypothyroid patient with persistent symptoms despite normal TSH on levothyroxine 100 µg asks about adding T3. Which is the source's most consistent response?
opts: Combination T4/T3 is not standard; review adherence and interactions first
Increase T4 dose beyond weight-based target
questions.exp: Combination therapy is not routinely recommended; first rule out adherence and drug interactions, then re-evaluate the diagnosis. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Persistent abnormal TFTs on adequate doses of levothyroxine are most often due to ___ or drug interactions.
questions.exp: Non-compliance is the most common cause of persistently abnormal TFTs on replacement; drug interactions and malabsorption are close seconds. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Assess these caveats: I Desiccated thyroid is the source's preferred long-term replacement. II Liothyronine has a longer half-life than levothyroxine.
questions.exp: Levothyroxine is the standard; liothyronine has a shorter half-life than levothyroxine. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among reversible causes of hypothyroidism that may allow taper?
questions.exp: Hashimoto is permanent; the others are typically transient and may allow cautious taper. (Book p909)

units.title: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features
units.sec: Causes of hypothyroidism and clinical features · p905
units.guide: Anchor the iatrogenic, drug-induced, iodine-related and autoimmune buckets. Learn why lithium, amiodarone, IFN-α and ICIs can each unmask or cause hypothyroidism, and tie constitutional, cardiovascular, reproductive and neurological features to common clinical presentations.

units.title: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism
units.sec: Hashimoto thyroiditis and subclinical hypothyroidism · p906
units.guide: Distinguish Hashimoto by histology, antibodies and demographic. Frame subclinical hypothyroidism as a TSH-guided decision tree with pregnancy-specific and antibody-positive thresholds that override simple numeric cut-offs.

units.title: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism
units.sec: Complications and clinical pearls of hypothyroidism · p907
units.guide: Read myxoedema coma, Hashimoto encephalopathy and carpal-tunnel syndrome as the principal complications. Note the page's 'hypocholesterolaemia' label is at odds with the usual hypercholesterolaemia of hypothyroidism and should be flagged as an inconsistency.

units.title: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations
units.sec: Hypothyroidism management: levothyroxine and special populations · p908
units.guide: Levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach with a 6–8 week TSH review after each dose change. Learn weight-based replacement in young adults, low-and-slow initiation in elderly cardiac patients and the 25–30% dose increase required in pregnancy.

units.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review
units.sec: Subclinical hypothyroidism, myxoedema coma and review · p909
units.guide: Recognise non-compliance as the most common cause of persistent abnormal TFTs and pursue IV levothyroxine plus hydrocortisone with passive rewarming for myxoedema coma. Combination T4/T3 therapy remains non-standard.
